addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- entire: Drive the Entire CLI (entire) for checkpoints, agent sessions, code provenance, and multi-agent review. Use when the user mentions Entire, checkpoints, session tracking, "entire why/blame/experts", agent activity recaps, or when a repo contains .entire/ and you need to inspect or manage tracked agent work.
- golang-patterns: Idiomatic Go patterns, best practices, and conventions for building robust, efficient, and maintainable Go applications. Use when writing or reviewing Go code and idiomatic structure or conventions are in question.
- golang-testing: Go testing patterns including table-driven tests, subtests, benchmarks, fuzzing, and test coverage. Follows TDD methodology with idiomatic Go practices. Use when writing Go tests — table-driven cases, subtests, benchmarks, fuzzing, or coverage.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.prompt:
I'm planning a new feature in the DevDesk TUI app (Go, Bubble Tea) at internal/ui/workspaces/. The feature: pressing "G" in the workspaces (ws) view enters a fuzzy-find search mode. The user types characters; once 3+ chars are typed, a list of paths (from the workspace tree) matching the fuzzy query appears. The user can move up/down in that list and press Enter to return to normal tree-browsing mode, positioned directly at the selected node (i.e., the tree expands/navigates to show that node selected).

I need a thorough understanding of the existing workspaces view code before planning this feature. Please investigate and report back (be thorough, quote code with file:line references):

1. **Model structure**: Read internal/ui/workspaces/model.go (or wherever Model is defined) — what fields exist, especially around tree state, current path, expanded nodes, selection, table/datatable usage, and any existing modal/mode state machine (e.g. `creating`, `editing`, `confirming` from CLAUDE.md, or `selectionMode`).

2. **Tree representation**: How is the workspace directory tree built and rendered as rows? Is it flattened into a table with indentation showing depth? Where's that logic (probably a file building "entries" or "rows" from the filesystem, and expand/collapse state)? Look for how a node/path is represented (a "row" type), and how "expand a specific path in the tree and select it" would need to work — i.e., is there already a function to navigate the tree to a specific path and mark it selected/scrolled-into-view?

3. **Update.go / key handling**: Read internal/ui/workspaces/update.go fully — how keys are dispatched (handleKeyMsg or similar), what existing state-based branching looks like (e.g. handleNormalKeyMsg vs handleSelectionKeyMsg per the earlier snippet I saw), and how mode switches are done. Also check what keys are already bound (uppercase letters per Rule 111 — need to confirm "G" is free/available for this view, cross-reference internal/ui/keymap package if referenced).

4. **View.go**: How is View() structured — does it delegate to different render functions based on mode? How would a full-screen or filter-bar-like search UI fit in (per Rule 112 forms-in-viewport pattern, or Rule 136 FilterBar pattern)?

5. **GetShortcuts() / help**: How are shortcuts declared for this view (Rule 130), and does it already implement help.Provider (Rule 114)?

6. **Existing filter/search in this view**: Does workspaces already have a FilterBar (Rule 136) or "/" search? If so read that code fully — this new fuzzy G-mode might reuse or parallel that pattern.

7. **datatable usage**: Confirm whether workspaces uses internal/ui/datatable (Rule 106/116/122) for its table, and how rows/columns are declared (file/dir/repo icon column per Rule 125).

Report file paths, line numbers, relevant code snippets, and a clear picture of the current architecture so I can design the fuzzy-find feature to fit existing patterns. Do not propose the implementation yourself — just report findings.

<result>I now have a comprehensive picture of the architecture. Here is the full report.

## 1. Model structure — `internal/ui/workspaces/model.go`

`Model` (lines 30-114) is **not** a general expand/collapse tree model. It is a **drill-down, single-level-at-a-time file browser**, closer to a classic file explorer than a tree view:

- `currentPath string` (line 39) — empty means workspaces root; otherwise the directory currently being listed.
- `listingPath string` (line 45) — the directory the *rows currently in the table* were actually read from. It can briefly differ from `currentPath` while a load is in flight; several handlers (`navigateIn`, `EntriesLoadedMsg` handling) guard on this to avoid races between two in-flight loads.
- `navigationStack []string` (line 46) and `cursorStack []int` (line 47) — breadcrumb/parent stack and per-level cursor positions, popped on `←`/`esc`.
- `pendingCursor int` (line 48) — cursor to restore after the async `loadEntries` lands (`-1` = none).
- `activeTabIndex int` (line 51) — which breadcrumb tab is highlighted.
- `mode ViewMode` (line 54) — the mode/state machine, values: `ModeNormal`, `ModeAdding`, `ModeConfirmingDelete`, `ModeRenaming`, `ModeSelecting`, `ModeConfirmingScanAll` (lines 20-27). This is exactly the `creating/editing/confirming`-style state machine referenced in project docs, just workspaces-specific naming.
- `input *WorkspaceInput`, `confirmModal *sharedcomponents.ConfirmModal`, `scanAllModal *sharedcomponents.OptionConfirmModal`, `pendingEntry *Entry` — the modal/form components tied to modes.
- `table datatable.Model[workspaceRow]` (line 35) — see §7 below.
- `scanCache`, `jobs`/`jobFrame`, `secrets`, `footer`, `deps`, `selectionMessage` — scan/job/secret/footer bookkeeping, not tree-relevant.

**Critical architectural fact: there is no in-memory representation of the whole workspace tree.** `loadEntries()` (`entries.go`... actually `table.go:60-126`) reads exactly one directory (`os.ReadDir`) per navigation step and replaces the table's rows. Nothing in the model holds "the tree" — expansion is simulated by navigating in and out, discarding the previous level's rows (except for cursor position, kept in `cursorStack`). There is no "expanded paths" set anywhere.

The closest thing to a recursive tree walk is `detectSubRepos`/`walkSubRepos` in `entry.go:112-195`, but that only discovers **git repository locations** nested under a directory (for S/F/A targeting), not a full listing of every file/dir path, and it does not build any row/UI representation — it returns `[]string` repo paths only.

## 2. Tree representation / rows

There is no "tree flattened into indented rows" — the table is always just the current directory's children, no indentation, no depth column. Row type: `workspaceRow` (`columns.go:35-48`):

```go
type workspaceRow struct {
    Entry Entry
    GitStatus string
    Sensitive secretsCell
    CI ciCell
    Critical, High, Medium, Low string
    Scanned string
}
```

`Entry` (`model.go:117-138`) is one filesystem entry: `Name`, `Path`, `ModTime`, `IsDir`, plus git metadata (`IsGitRepo`, `GitBranch`, etc.) and `SubRepoPaths`/`SubRepoSkipped` for aggregation when the entry is a non-git directory.

**There is no existing function that "expands the tree to a specific path and selects it."** Navigation only ever moves one level at a time via `navigateIn()`/`navigateUp()` (`update.go:319-366`), each triggering a fresh `loadEntries()` Cmd. To land on an arbitrary nested path, a new feature would need to synthesize the intermediate `navigationStack`/`cursorStack` state and either (a) issue a chain of loads level-by-level, or (b) directly build `currentPath` = the parent of the target, `navigationStack` = all its ancestors, then load and set `pendingCursor` to the matching row once `EntriesLoadedMsg` lands. Nothing like this exists today — it would be new code.

`rowsFor(entries []Entry)` (`table.go`/`columns.go:167-197`) decorates entries into rows (adds scan/spinner state); `setEntries` (`table.go:23-26`) calls `m.table.SetItems` + `Remeasure()`; `refreshRows` (`table.go:36-38`) rebuilds rows without remeasuring (used for spinner ticks).

## 3. update.go — key handling

Full file read: `internal/ui/workspaces/update.go`.

- `Init()` (17-26) kicks off `loadEntries()`, `loadScanCacheCmd()`, and (in `ModeNormal`) `checkDepsCmd`.
- `InEditMode()` (29-31): `m.mode != ModeNormal || m.table.InEditMode()` — used by the router to block `ctrl+p` etc. while a form/filter has focus.
- `FilterBarVisible()` (34-36) implements `app.FilterBarView`.
- Top-level `Update()` (39-192): a big `switch msg.(type)`, with `tea.KeyMsg` delegated immediately to `handleKeyMsg` (line 48-49). All other messages are handled and fall through to `m.footer.Handle(msg)` (184) then, **only in `ModeNormal`**, `m.table.Update(msg)` (187-189).
- `handleKeyMsg` (194-280) is the dispatcher, in strict priority order (mirrors Rule 130's "mode replaces the whole vocabulary"):
  1. `m.table.InEditMode()` (filter bar `/` search) → delegate to `m.table.Update(msg)` and return (197-199).
  2. `ModeAdding` → delegate to `m.input.Update` (202-206).
  3. `ModeConfirmingDelete` → delegate to `m.confirmModal.Update` (209-213).
  4. `ModeConfirmingScanAll` → delegate to `m.scanAllModal.Update` (216-220).
  5. `ModeRenaming` → delegate to `m.input.Update` (223-227).
  6. `ModeSelecting` → `handleSelectionKeyMsg` (230-232, defined 369-392).
  7. Otherwise, **normal mode** switch on `msg.String()` (239-277):
     ```go
     a := m.actions()
     switch msg.String() {
     case "/": return m, m.table.Update(msg)
     case "enter": return m.guard(a.Enter, m.openScanDetails)
     case "ctrl+r": return m, m.loadEntries()
     case keymap.New: return m.startAdd()
     case keymap.Rename: return m.guard(a.Rename, m.startRename)
     case keymap.Delete: return m.guard(a.Delete, m.startDelete)
     case keymap.Terminal: return m.openTerminal()
     case keymap.IDE: return m.openIDE()
     case keymap.Web: return m.guard(a.Web, m.openInBrowser)
     case keymap.Scan: return m.guard(a.Scan, m.startSecurityScan)
     case keymap.Fetch: return m.guard(a.Sync, m.startSync)
     case keymap.ScanAll: return m.guard(a.All, m.confirmScanAll)
     case keymap.Copy: return m.guard(a.Copy, m.copyPath)
     case "left": return m.navigateUp()
     case "right": return m.navigateIn()
     case "esc": return m.navigateUp()
     case "up", "down", "pgup", "pgdown", "home", "end": return m, m.table.Update(msg)
     }
     return m, nil
     ```
     **Any key not explicitly listed (e.g. "G") currently does nothing** — it falls through to `return m, nil` at line 279. So a new mode-switch key needs its own `case`.

- `m.actions()` (`availability.go:73-147`) computes an `actionSet` of `shortcut.Availability` per action, consulted both by `GetShortcuts()` (for greying out, Rule 130) and by `guard()` (for refusing with a footer warning) — "one computation, two readers."

Mode-switch helpers: `startAdd()` (405-409, sets `mode = ModeAdding`, builds `*WorkspaceInput`), `startDelete()` (412-438), `startRename()` (441-450) — all follow the same shape: set `m.mode`, build the component, return `(m, nil)`. A fuzzy-find mode would likely follow this exact shape (a new `ModeFuzzyFind` and a new component field).

**Keymap check (item 3's "is G free")**: `internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go` declares the global uppercase action vocabulary (`New="N"`, `Edit="E"`, ... `Get="G"` at line 73: `// Pull (get) the image or tag`). Per `.claude/rules/tui-layout.md` Rule 111, an uppercase letter's meaning is global across the whole app — `G` is already "Pull (get)", used elsewhere (oci_resources/registry views), not currently used in workspaces itself, but **not free** by the declared vocabulary. The only declared-free uppercase letters are `J`, `Q`, `Z` (`keymap.go:176`, `Free()`). So binding "G" to a new "fuzzy-find" action in workspaces would collide with the app-wide meaning of `G` ("Pull/get") per Rule 111, even though nothing in the workspaces package currently binds it. Lowercase `g` is also not free by default — Rule 111 states vim aliases `h j k l g G` were removed entirely and are not local-toggle material either, though the rule notes `g` was reinstated *only* in the document viewer as a "go to line" local toggle (`localToggles` in `keymap.go:208`), a case explicitly justified as "not a bending of the rule" because it takes an argument. Workspaces is not in that `localToggles` list. Both uppercase `G` (reserved for Get) and unregistered lowercase `g` are exceptions/collisions that would need to be resolved against Rule 111 before implementation (not proposing a fix, just flagging it per your ask).

Also worth noting: `internal/ui/keymap/keymap_test.go`/`announced_test.go` has `TestEveryAnnouncedActionIsBoundInItsPackage`, `TestNoAnnouncementSpellsAnActionOutInFull`, `TestEveryAnnouncedToggleIsBoundInItsPackage`, and presumably (referenced in project-context.md) `TestNoBareLetterIsNavigation` / `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` / `TestOnlyThreeCtrlCombinationsSurvive` — these are static source-scanning tests that will fail the build if an uppercase key is bound without being in the `keymap` vocabulary, or if a `{Key: "G", ...}` shortcut/help announcement doesn't match a `case keymap.X:` binding.

## 4. view.go — View() structure

`internal/ui/workspaces/view.go`, `View()` (29-80): a straight-line sequence of mode checks, each returning a full-screen `lipgloss.Place`-centered overlay for its mode, in the same priority order as `handleKeyMsg`:

```go
func (m Model) View() string {
    if m.mode == ModeAdding && m.input != nil { return lipgloss.Place(...) }        // centered overlay
    if m.mode == ModeConfirmingDelete && m.confirmModal != nil { return lipgloss.Place(...) }
    if m.mode == ModeConfirmingScanAll && m.scanAllModal != nil { return lipgloss.Place(...) }
    if m.mode == ModeRenaming && m.input != nil { return lipgloss.Place(...) }
    if m.error != "" { return contentStyle.Render(...) }
    return m.renderTable()   // renderTable() -> m.table.View()
}
```

Note this actually contradicts Rule 112 as literally documented (`docs/architecture` doesn't say this, but `.claude/rules/tui-layout.md` Rule 112 says **creation/edit forms must be in the main viewport, not a modal** — yet `ModeAdding`/`ModeRenaming` here use `lipgloss.Place(... Center, Center ...)`, i.e. a centered overlay, same as the confirm modals). This is a pre-existing pattern in workspaces that appears to diverge from Rule 112's stated ideal — worth flagging since your new G-mode UI should decide deliberately whether to mimic this existing centered-overlay pattern or the more sanctioned full-viewport form pattern.

`GetFooterHeight()`/`RenderFooter()` (87-121) implement Rule 124's footer layout: filter bar (when visible) + breadcrumb tab bar + blank line + info line, based on `m.table.FilterBar().ExtraHeight()`. A fuzzy-find search UI, if it reuses the filter-bar-at-bottom pattern (Rule 136), would need analogous plumbing here; if it's instead a full "search mode" replacing the whole table view (more like `ModeAdding`), it would instead add a branch to `View()` similar to the other modes and adjust `GetFooterHeight()`/`RenderFooter()` accordingly for that mode.

`renderTabBar()` (134-148) renders the drill-down breadcrumb from `navigationStack` + `currentPath` — this is what "positioned at the selected node" ultimately needs to reflect once a fuzzy-search jump lands (the breadcrumb must show the new ancestor chain).

## 5. GetShortcuts() / help — `view.go:413-576`

`GetShortcuts()` (413-480) is mode-aware exactly per Rule 130: an early-return block per mode (`ModeAdding`, `ModeRenaming`, `ModeConfirmingDelete`, `ModeSelecting`), then the normal-mode list built from `m.actions()` with `Disabled: !a.X.Enabled()` on each row-dependent action. A new fuzzy-find mode would need its own early-return block here (e.g., "↑↓ Move", "enter Select", "esc Cancel").

`GetHelpContent()` (506-576) implements `help.Content`/`help.KeyBinding`/`help.Section` — confirms the view implements `help.Provider`. It documents the drill-down model explicitly: *"The browser uses a drill-down model. Press → on a directory to see its contents. Press ← to go back."* (541-543) — this is the authoritative doc-comment confirming there is no tree/expand model today.

`GetTitle()`, `GetIcon()`, `GetHeaderInfo()` (482-503) round out the header interface.

## 6. Existing filter/search — `/` FilterBar

Workspaces **does** already have a `/`-triggered filter, via `internal/ui/datatable`'s embedded `components.FilterBar` (`internal/ui/components/filter_bar.go`), **not** a workspaces-specific implementation:

- `datatable.Model[T]` owns a `bar components.FilterBar` (`datatable.go:221`), created in `datatable.New` (`datatable.go:282-284`).
- `datatable.Model.Update` (`datatable.go:538-589`) delegates to `m.bar.Update(msg)` when `m.bar.InEditMode()`, and handles `"/"` (line 555-562, calls `m.bar.ActivateSearch()`, refusing if `!m.Searchable()`) and `"."` (CycleSort) itself; navigation keys (`up/down/pgup/pgdown/home/end`) move the underlying `bubbles/table`.
- `FilterBar` (components/filter_bar.go) is a **substring** matcher over whatever columns declare a `Search` func (in workspaces: `Name` and `Remote`, see `columns.go:96,101` — `Search: func(r workspaceRow) string { return r.Entry.Name }`). It is a single-line textinput bar rendered at the bottom (`View()`, lines 189-220), 2 extra footer lines when visible (`ExtraHeight()`).
- Crucially: **this filters only the rows currently loaded — i.e. the current directory's immediate children** — not a recursive fuzzy search of the whole workspace tree. It's a different feature than what you're planning (single-level substring filter vs. multi-level fuzzy path search), though its bar-at-the-bottom UI/state machine (`searching` bool, `textinput.Model`, `ActivateSearch`/`esc`/`enter` handling) is a reasonable template to study for the "type characters, live-update a result list, Enter to confirm" interaction shape.
- `Model.entries()` (`table.go:41-47`) reconstructs `[]Entry` straight from `m.table.Items()` — i.e., from whatever the filter bar currently shows — used by `selectedEntry()` (`table.go:55-58`) to resolve cursor→row safely under a filter (this guards against the historical bug D24 mentioned at `table.go:51-54`, where an action indexed the unfiltered list with a filtered cursor).

There is no existing "/" or other search that walks the whole tree recursively and returns cross-directory path results — the closest analog for "walk everything" is `detectSubRepos`/`walkSubRepos` (`entry.go`), but as noted, that only discovers git-repo roots, not general paths, and returns no UI-ready rows.

## 7. datatable usage — Rule 106/116/122/125

Confirmed: `internal/ui/workspaces` uses the generic `internal/ui/datatable` package.

- `Model.table datatable.Model[workspaceRow]` (`model.go:35`), constructed in `New()` (`model.go:144-156`) via `datatable.New(datatable.Config[workspaceRow]{Columns: workspaceColumns(cfg.Scan.EnableCIScore), SortColumn: -1})`.
- Columns declared in `columns.go` (`workspaceColumns`, lines 79-126): icon column with no title (leftmost, `MinWidth: datatable.IconColumnWidth`, `Cell: func(r) string { return entryIcon(r.Entry) }`, `Style:` colored via `theme.IconStyle(entryIconRole(r.Entry))`) — this is exactly the Rule 125 file/dir/repo icon column pattern the user mentioned, backed by `internal/ui/fileicon` and documented in `docs/architecture/workspaces.md`. Then `Name` (searchable, `SizingContent`), `Remote` (searchable, truncate-head, flex), `Git Status`, `Secrets`, four severity count columns (`C H M L` via the shared `count()` helper), `CI` (optional, inserted conditionally when `withCI`), `Scanned`, `Modified`.
- Rows are plain-text cells with separate `Style func(r) lipgloss.Style` callbacks (never `style.Render()` baked into cell text) — consistent with Rule 122 ("NEVER use style.Render() inside table.Row{}").
- `updateTableSize()` (`table.go:15-17`) calls `m.table.Resize(...)`, and `setEntries`/`refreshRows` (`table.go:23-38`) call `SetItems`/`Remeasure` — the Rule 116 width-solving arithmetic lives inside `datatable` (`widths.go`), not duplicated in workspaces.

---

### Summary of what a fuzzy-find "G-mode" would have to reconcile with existing architecture (facts only, no proposal)

1. **No tree state exists to "expand."** Navigation is one-level-at-a-time via `os.ReadDir` in `loadEntries()`; there's no cached/loaded representation of the whole workspace tree, no expanded-paths set, and no existing "navigate to arbitrary nested path and select it" function — that would be new machinery layered on top of `currentPath`/`navigationStack`/`cursorStack`/`pendingCursor`.
2. **A full-tree fuzzy search needs its own recursive filesystem walk** (something like `walkSubRepos` in shape, but collecting all paths, not just repo roots) — nothing today builds that list.
3. **`G` is already claimed** by the app-wide uppercase vocabulary (`keymap.Get`, "Pull (get) the image or tag") per Rule 111; declared-free uppercase letters are only `J`, `Q`, `Z`. Lowercase `g` is also not declared as a workspaces local toggle in `keymap.localToggles`.
4. **The mode-switch shape to follow** is the existing `ViewMode` enum + `mode`/component-pointer field pattern (`ModeAdding`/`WorkspaceInput` is the closest precedent for "a component that owns its own key handling while a mode flag is set"), dispatched with top priority in `handleKeyMsg`, mirrored in `View()`, `GetShortcuts()`, and `GetFooterHeight()`/`RenderFooter()`.
5. **Existing `/` FilterBar is a *different* feature** (single-directory substring filter, not a cross-tree fuzzy finder) but is the closest UI/interaction precedent in this package for "type into a bar, get a live-updating list."
6. **Rule 112 tension**: workspaces' own `ModeAdding`/`ModeRenaming` already render as centered overlays rather than full-viewport forms, which is worth being aware of as precedent (or as a deviation) when deciding how the new search UI should be laid out.</result>

## 1. Model structure — `internal/ui/workspaces/model.go`

`Model` (lines 30-114) is **not** a general expand/collapse tree model. It is a **drill-down, single-level-at-a-time file browser**, closer to a classic file explorer than a tree view:

- `currentPath string` (line 39) — empty means workspaces root; otherwise the directory currently being listed.
- `listingPath string` (line 45) — the directory the *rows currently in the table* were actually read from. It can briefly differ from `currentPath` while a load is in flight; several handlers (`navigateIn`, `EntriesLoadedMsg` handling) guard on this to avoid races between two in-flight loads.
- `navigationStack []string` (line 46) and `cursorStack []int` (line 47) — breadcrumb/parent stack and per-level cursor positions, popped on `←`/`esc`.
- `pendingCursor int` (line 48) — cursor to restore after the async `loadEntries` lands (`-1` = none).
- `activeTabIndex int` (line 51) — which breadcrumb tab is highlighted.
- `mode ViewMode` (line 54) — the mode/state machine, values: `ModeNormal`, `ModeAdding`, `ModeConfirmingDelete`, `ModeRenaming`, `ModeSelecting`, `ModeConfirmingScanAll` (lines 20-27). This is exactly the `creating/editing/confirming`-style state machine referenced in project docs, just workspaces-specific naming.
- `input *WorkspaceInput`, `confirmModal *sharedcomponents.ConfirmModal`, `scanAllModal *sharedcomponents.OptionConfirmModal`, `pendingEntry *Entry` — the modal/form components tied to modes.
- `table datatable.Model[workspaceRow]` (line 35) — see §7 below.
- `scanCache`, `jobs`/`jobFrame`, `secrets`, `footer`, `deps`, `selectionMessage` — scan/job/secret/footer bookkeeping, not tree-relevant.

**Critical architectural fact: there is no in-memory representation of the whole workspace tree.** `loadEntries()` (`entries.go`... actually `table.go:60-126`) reads exactly one directory (`os.ReadDir`) per navigation step and replaces the table's rows. Nothing in the model holds "the tree" — expansion is simulated by navigating in and out, discarding the previous level's rows (except for cursor position, kept in `cursorStack`). There is no "expanded paths" set anywhere.

The closest thing to a recursive tree walk is `detectSubRepos`/`walkSubRepos` in `entry.go:112-195`, but that only discovers **git repository locations** nested under a directory (for S/F/A targeting), not a full listing of every file/dir path, and it does not build any row/UI representation — it returns `[]string` repo paths only.

## 2. Tree representation / rows

There is no "tree flattened into indented rows" — the table is always just the current directory's children, no indentation, no depth column. Row type: `workspaceRow` (`columns.go:35-48`):

```go
type workspaceRow struct {
    Entry Entry
    GitStatus string
    Sensitive secretsCell
    CI ciCell
    Critical, High, Medium, Low string
    Scanned string
}
```

`Entry` (`model.go:117-138`) is one filesystem entry: `Name`, `Path`, `ModTime`, `IsDir`, plus git metadata (`IsGitRepo`, `GitBranch`, etc.) and `SubRepoPaths`/`SubRepoSkipped` for aggregation when the entry is a non-git directory.

**There is no existing function that "expands the tree to a specific path and selects it."** Navigation only ever moves one level at a time via `navigateIn()`/`navigateUp()` (`update.go:319-366`), each triggering a fresh `loadEntries()` Cmd. To land on an arbitrary nested path, a new feature would need to synthesize the intermediate `navigationStack`/`cursorStack` state and either (a) issue a chain of loads level-by-level, or (b) directly build `currentPath` = the parent of the target, `navigationStack` = all its ancestors, then load and set `pendingCursor` to the matching row once `EntriesLoadedMsg` lands. Nothing like this exists today — it would be new code.

`rowsFor(entries []Entry)` (`table.go`/`columns.go:167-197`) decorates entries into rows (adds scan/spinner state); `setEntries` (`table.go:23-26`) calls `m.table.SetItems` + `Remeasure()`; `refreshRows` (`table.go:36-38`) rebuilds rows without remeasuring (used for spinner ticks).

### Summary of what a fuzzy-find "G-mode" would have to reconcile with existing architecture (facts only, no proposal)

1. **No tree state exists to "expand."** Navigation is one-level-at-a-time via `os.ReadDir` in `loadEntries()`; there's no cached/loaded representation of the whole workspace tree, no expanded-paths set, and no existing "navigate to arbitrary nested path and select it" function — that would be new machinery layered on top of `currentPath`/`navigationStack`/`cursorStack`/`pendingCursor`.
2. **A full-tree fuzzy search needs its own recursive filesystem walk** (something like `walkSubRepos` in shape, but collecting all paths, not just repo roots) — nothing today builds that list.
3. **`G` is already claimed** by the app-wide uppercase vocabulary (`keymap.Get`, "Pull (get) the image or tag") per Rule 111; declared-free uppercase letters are only `J`, `Q`, `Z`. Lowercase `g` is also not declared as a workspaces local toggle in `keymap.localToggles`.

5. **Existing `/` FilterBar is a *different* feature** (single-directory substring filter, not a cross-tree fuzzy finder) but is the closest UI/interaction precedent in this package for "type into a bar, get a live-updating list."

# Research Report: fuzzy-find "G" mode in the workspaces view

## 1. Keymap vocabulary (`internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go`)

The package declares **three disjoint namespaces** plus a fourth (modal) one (doc comment `internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go:9-19`):
- Uppercase letter = action, meaning is **global** to the whole app.
- Lowercase letter = filter/display toggle, meaning is **local** per declared surface.
- Everything else (arrows, esc, `/`, `.`, `?`, `:`…) is structural.

The full 23-action uppercase table (`internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go:56-83`, mirrored in `.claude/rules/tui-layout.md:68-75`):

| Key | Const | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| N | New | Create a resource from this context |
| E | Edit | Edit the selected resource |
| D | Delete | Delete the selected resource |
| M | Rename | Rename (mv) |
| S | Scan | Scan the selected target |
| A | ScanAll | Scan everything (modal w/ purge checkbox) |
| F | Fetch | Catch up with the source: fetch + fast-forward, or follow a stream |
| C | Clone | Enter clone selection |
| T | Terminal | Open a terminal or shell |
| O | IDE | Open in the configured IDE |
| W | Web | Open a URL in the browser |
| L | Logs | Open the logs |
| V | Pager | Open in the system pager |
| K | Kill | Stop, kill |
| P | Prune | Remove unused resources |
| B | Browser | Open the multi-registry browser |
| **G** | **Get** | **Pull (get) the image or tag** |
| U | Auth | Login/logout of the registry |
| X | Exclude | Add to .gitleaksignore |
| R | Requests | Open merge requests · PRs |
| I | Issues | Open issues |
| H | Diagnose | Open network diagnostics on this target |
| Y | Copy | Copy the obvious thing to clipboard |

**`G` is `Get`, and its scope is global, not per-view.** Per the doc comment (`keymap.go:11-13`): "An UPPERCASE letter is an action, and its meaning is global to the application." There is no per-view opt-in mechanism — the enforcement test only checks that any uppercase letter bound in a view's key-switch matches *some* entry in this one global table (`IsAction(key)`), not that its meaning is contextually appropriate for that view. So mechanically the test wouldn't block a second, different meaning for `G`, but it would directly violate the package's stated design invariant ("`D` deletes, in every view, whatever 'delete' means wherever you are" — same for `G`).

I confirmed **`keymap.Get`/`G` is currently bound in exactly one package**, `internal/ui/oci_resources` (Docker/OCI registry browser):
- `internal/ui/oci_resources/browser_keys.go:212` — `case keymap.Get:` (handler)
- `internal/ui/oci_resources/view.go:260` — `{Key: keymap.Get, Description: "Pull image"}` (shortcut announcement)
- also referenced in `browser_search_test.go:659,747` and `update_test.go:339`

I confirmed **`internal/ui/workspaces` does not currently use `G`/`keymap.Get` anywhere**. Full list of uppercase actions workspaces currently binds (`internal/ui/workspaces/update.go:246-267`, `view.go:465-525`): `N, M, D, T, O, W, S, F, A, Y`. `G` is free of use there, but not free in the global vocabulary.

### Free letters
`internal/ui/keymap/keymap.go:176`:
```go
var free = []string{"J", "Q", "Z"}
```
returned by `Free()`. These are the **only** uppercase letters with no assigned meaning anywhere in the app. `TestFreeLettersAreActuallyFree` (`keymap_test.go:79-89`) asserts `len(actions) + len(free) == 26` — i.e. every letter is either used or declared free, none is undeclared. **`G` is not free** — it is claimed by `Get`/Pull, used in `oci_resources`.

### `DeclaredExceptions()` / `retiredAliases`
- `DeclaredExceptions()` (`keymap.go:266-268`) returns two hand-written deviations from the vocabulary rule, each with a French-language justification (`keymap.go:246-263`):
  - `o` in `security/results/ci-tab` — open the CI pipeline (a lowercase letter used as an action because burning a global uppercase letter for a single-tab action costs more than it gains).
  - `ctrl+y` in `oci/launch-form` — copy the `docker run` command.
- `retiredAliases` (`keymap_test.go:62`) = `map[string]bool{"j": true, "k": true}` — vim leftovers with no surviving meaning; `g` (lowercase) was explicitly *removed* from this list in §3.53 because it regained a meaning in the viewer (the "go to line" prompt — see §5 below). **`G` (uppercase) was never in `retiredAliases`** — it's in `actions`, not a retired vim alias — but the historical comment at `keymap.go:170-176` and `keymap_test.go:54-61`/Rule 111 doc (`.claude/rules/tui-layout.md:24-38`) explicitly documents that the vim aliases `h j k l g G` were **removed entirely** application-wide (§3.26), and `TestNoBareLetterIsNavigation` (`keymap_test.go:139-163`) forbids any bare letter being bound alongside navigation keys (`up/down/left/right/pgup/pgdown/home/end`) in the same case-switch clause.

### How a view "reserves" a letter
There is **no per-view registry/opt-in file** for uppercase letters — the single global `actions` map in `keymap.go` *is* the registry, and any uppercase-letter binding anywhere in the code is checked against it by AST scan. There is a `Surface`/`localToggles` mechanism (`keymap.go:192-234`), but it is exclusively for **lowercase** toggles, matched by longest path-prefix (e.g. `{"viewer", "ui/viewer/", []string{"f","c","w","v","t","n","g","s"}}` at `keymap.go:208`). Uppercase actions have no analogous per-surface table — they are inherently global.

## Central enforcement tests (`internal/ui/keymap/keymap_test.go`, `internal/ui/keymap/announced_test.go`)

Both files work by AST-parsing every `.go` file under `internal/app` and `internal/ui` (excluding `_test.go` and the keymap package itself, `scannedTrees` at `keymap_test.go:23-26`), looking for `switch` statements that look like key switches (contain a structural key or a ctrl+/alt+/shift+ combo, `isKeySwitch` at `keymap_test.go:363-375`), and for `{Key: ..., Description: ...}` composite literals (shortcut/help announcements).

Relevant tests, all of which **would run against any new `G` binding in workspaces**:
- `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` (`keymap_test.go:108-129`) — **the central test**. Any uppercase letter in a key-switch clause must satisfy `IsAction(key)` (or be a modal Y/N). Since `IsAction("G")` is already `true` (it's `Get`), binding `G` in workspaces for "fuzzy find" would **pass this test mechanically** — it doesn't check that the *meaning* matches; it only checks the letter is declared *somewhere*. This is a gap between the letter of the test and the spirit of the design doc.
- `TestNoBareLetterIsNavigation` (`keymap_test.go:139-163`) — forbids `G`/`g` (or any letter) appearing in the same switch clause as `up/down/...` or in `retiredAliases`. Not an issue as long as `G` isn't aliased to navigation.
- `TestEveryLowercaseBindingIsDeclared` (`keymap_test.go:197-229`) — n/a for uppercase `G`, but relevant if the design instead used a **lowercase** letter locally in workspaces (would need a `localToggles` entry for `ui/workspaces/`, which doesn't currently exist at all — workspaces has zero declared local lowercase toggles).

## 2. Fuzzy matching — none exists

`grep -rli "fuzzy"` across the entire repository (all Go files) returned **zero matches**. `go.mod`/`go.sum` contain no fuzzy-matching library (no `sahilm/fuzzy`, `lithammer/fuzzysearch`, `junegunn/fzf`-style dep, etc. — only Bubble Tea/Lipgloss/Chroma/etc., see `go.mod:1-24`).

The only existing text-matching logic in the shared table infrastructure is `datatable.Model[T].matchesQuery` (`internal/ui/datatable/datatable.go:813-829`), which is a **plain case-insensitive substring match** (`strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(value), query)`), tried per searchable column and then against all searchable columns joined. This is *not* fuzzy (no subsequence/edit-distance/scoring). **A fuzzy-find feature would need to implement its own scoring algorithm from scratch** — there is nothing to reuse.

## 5. "Jump to node" / "reveal in tree" — no such logic exists anywhere in the app

This is the most consequential finding for the design. I searched broadly (`reveal`, `ancestor`, `expand`, `Flatten`) across the whole `internal/ui` tree and read the workspaces model, the viewer's tree, and the forge explorer's selection logic.

**Workspaces is not a flattened tree at all.** It is a single-level directory browser with drill-down/drill-up (`internal/ui/workspaces/model.go:38-49`):
```go
currentPath     string   // "" = root, else the current directory
listingPath     string
navigationStack []string // breadcrumb stack of parent paths
cursorStack     []int    // cursor per level, restored on navigate-up
pendingCursor   int
```
Each keypress that drills down (`→`) replaces the table's entire row set with a fresh `loadEntries()` read of one directory (`internal/ui/workspaces/table.go:63-90`, `setEntries` at `table.go:22-27`); there is no in-memory flattened multi-level tree of all workspace paths. **Consequence for the design**: a fuzzy-search result pointing at a nested path cannot simply "select a row" — the view would need to synthesize the breadcrumb stack (`navigationStack`) and issue a sequence of directory loads down to the target, since only one level's `Entry` rows exist in the table at a time. This is new logic; nothing in workspaces solves it today.

**The one real tree in the app** is the document viewer's JSON/XML tree (`internal/ui/viewer/tree.go`), backed by `viewer.Flatten(root *Node, collapsed map[int]bool) []FlatNode` (`internal/viewer/node.go:58`) and a `collapsed map[int]bool` keyed by node ID (`internal/ui/viewer/model.go:85`). It supports single-node `toggleNode(expand bool)` (`tree.go:118-137`) driven by `←`/`→` on the *currently selected* row — but there is **no "given an ID/path, expand every ancestor and set the cursor to it" function**. Nothing walks up from a target node clearing `collapsed[ancestorID]` for each ancestor.

**The closest analog to a "jump to a location by typed query" UX** is the viewer's **`g` "go to line"** prompt (lowercase, not uppercase — `internal/ui/viewer/goto.go`):
- `activateGoto()` (`goto.go:38-43`) opens a prompt in the filter-bar's slot.
- `submitGoto()` (`goto.go:76-101`) parses a line number, looks it up in `rowOfLine map[int]int` (populated by `text.go:33,55` from the rendered pane's line→row mapping), and calls `m.textViewport.SetYOffset(row)` — i.e., it scrolls to a **precomputed row offset**, not a tree node; it does not expand any tree state, and if the target row is filtered out it reports "Line %d is hidden by the filter" rather than trying to reveal it (`goto.go:94-97`). This confirms the codebase's existing precedent for "jump to X" is scroll-to-known-offset, not expand-ancestors-and-select — the latter would be new.
- Design-history note directly on point (`.claude/rules/tui-layout.md:30-38`, `keymap.go` comment at line ~176): lowercase `g` in the viewer was explicitly re-legitimized specifically *because* "the jump takes an **argument**", which is exactly the shape a `G`-triggered fuzzy find in workspaces would also have — but that argument-taking exception was granted to a **lowercase** letter (`g`), not the uppercase `G` action letter, and it lives in `retiredAliases`'s counter-example discussion, not in the `actions` table.

**Other views checked, none relevant:**
- `oci_resources/registry_browser.go` — a checkbox/expand-groups picker over registries (`buildEntries`, `toggleGroup`), not a searchable flattened path tree.
- `internal/ui/forge/explorer/selection.go` — `cloneSelection.includes(path)` walks **up** a path's ancestors to test set membership (nearest marked ancestor wins, `selection.go:31-47`) for a checkbox-style multi-select UI, not for revealing/expanding a tree UI to a specific node. Reusable *idea* (walking `parentPath` iteratively) but not a UI-reveal mechanism.
- `internal/ui/security/inventory.go` and friends — flat findings/inventory tables, no tree structure at all.

**Conclusion for §5**: there is no existing "expand ancestors and select a row in a flattened tree" pattern anywhere in the codebase to reuse or mirror. The nearest building blocks are (a) `viewer.Flatten` + `collapsed map[int]bool` as the general shape for a flattened, collapsible tree, and (b) the `g`/goto-line prompt as the UX precedent for "a letter that opens a prompt taking an argument, distinct from navigation." Both would need new code for a workspaces path-reveal feature; workspaces' current one-level-at-a-time directory model is likely the biggest structural gap to address in the design.

| S | Scan | Scan the selected target |

| W | Web | Open a URL in the browser |
| L | Logs | Open the logs |
| V | Pager | Open in the system pager |

| P | Prune | Remove unused resources |

| U | Auth | Login/logout of the registry |
| X | Exclude | Add to .gitleaksignore |
| R | Requests | Open merge requests · PRs |
| I | Issues | Open issues |
| H | Diagnose | Open network diagnostics on this target |

Because this is a **narrowing filter over an already-loaded, already-rendered row set** (and workspaces only ever has one directory level's rows loaded at a time — see §5), FilterBar is architecturally different from what a "fuzzy find across an entire tree of paths, possibly several levels deep, producing a distinct results list with scores" would need. Reusing FilterBar's `/` slot/rendering conventions (2-line frame, `BarFrame`, `esc`/`enter` semantics) is plausible for visual consistency, but its `searchQuery`/live-filter model does not by itself support "switch to a different result-list mode with a different item type and jump target," which the design will need to build separately.

## 4. datatable (`internal/ui/datatable/datatable.go`) — Column/Model API summary

```go
type Sizing int
const ( SizingUnset Sizing = iota; SizingFixed; SizingContent )

type Column[T any] struct {
    Title        string
    Sizing       Sizing   // no default — TestEveryColumnDeclaresItsSizing rejects unset
    MinWidth     int      // fixed width, or content floor
    MaxWidth     int      // content ceiling, 0 = none
    Optional     bool     // droppable when the table doesn't fit
    DropFirst    bool     // dropped before other Optional columns
    TruncateHead bool     // cut the start instead of the end (paths/URLs/refs)
    Flex         int      // share of leftover space
    Cell      func(T) string             // plain text only, measured/truncated first
    Style     func(T) lipgloss.Style     // applied after measuring
    Cut       func(T) int                // splits cell into two styled runs
    TailStyle func(T) lipgloss.Style
    Less   func(a, b T) bool  // nil = not sortable
    Search func(T) string     // nil = not searched
}

type Config[T any] struct {
    Columns        []Column[T]
    Tokens         []components.FilterToken
    TokenMatch     func(item T, active map[string]bool) bool
    SortColumn     int
    SortDesc       bool
    Key            func(T) string    // identity for the busy-row facility
    StatusColumn   int
    SelectedStyles func(T) table.Styles
}

func New[T any](cfg Config[T]) Model[T]
func (m *Model[T]) SetItems(items []T)
func (m *Model[T]) Remeasure()
func (m *Model[T]) Items() []T
func (m *Model[T]) Visible() []T
func (m *Model[T]) Selected() (T, bool)
func (m *Model[T]) Cursor() int
func (m *Model[T]) SetCursor(i int)
func (m *Model[T]) GotoTop()
func (m *Model[T]) FilterBar() *components.FilterBar
func (m *Model[T]) InEditMode() bool
func (m *Model[T]) Searchable() bool
func (m *Model[T]) Table() *table.Model
func (m *Model[T]) SetHeight(h int)
func (m *Model[T]) Focus() / Blur()
func (m *Model[T]) Resize(width, height int)       // Rule 116 width solver
func (m *Model[T]) CycleSort() / SetSort(column int, desc bool) / SortState() (int, bool)
func (m *Model[T]) Update(msg tea.Msg) tea.Cmd      // owns up/down/pgup/pgdown/home/end/"/"/"."
func (m *Model[T]) MarkBusy/ClearBusy/IsBusy(key string) / BusyLabels() []string
func (m *Model[T]) AdvanceSpinner()
func (m *Model[T]) SetTokenActive(label string, active bool) / IsTokenActive(label string) bool
```

For a fuzzy-results list (path + score, maybe highlighted match spans), this generic `Model[T]` is directly reusable: define a `matchRow{ Path string; Score int; ... }` type, build `[]datatable.Column[matchRow]` with a path column (`SizingContent`, `TruncateHead: true` likely, since two paths sharing a prefix are told apart by their tail — this is exactly the pattern already used for URLs/image refs per the `TruncateHead` doc comment at `datatable.go:99-106`), and a `New(Config[matchRow]{...})`. Note `Model[T].Update` already claims `/`, `.`, and the navigation keys — a separate fuzzy-results-mode table instance would need its own key handling in the parent view rather than colliding with the primary workspaces table's own `Update`.

## 5. "Jump to node" / "reveal in tree" — no such logic exists anywhere in the app

This is the most consequential finding for the design. I searched broadly (`reveal`, `ancestor`, `expand`, `Flatten`) across the whole `internal/ui` tree and read the workspaces model, the viewer's tree, and the forge explorer's selection logic.

**Workspaces is not a flattened tree at all.** It is a single-level directory browser with drill-down/drill-up (`internal/ui/workspaces/model.go:38-49`):
```go
currentPath     string   // "" = root, else the current directory
listingPath     string
navigationStack []string // breadcrumb stack of parent paths
cursorStack     []int    // cursor per level, restored on navigate-up
pendingCursor   int
```
Each keypress that drills down (`→`) replaces the table's entire row set with a fresh `loadEntries()` read of one directory (`internal/ui/workspaces/table.go:63-90`, `setEntries` at `table.go:22-27`); there is no in-memory flattened multi-level tree of all workspace paths. **Consequence for the design**: a fuzzy-search result pointing at a nested path cannot simply "select a row" — the view would need to synthesize the breadcrumb stack (`navigationStack`) and issue a sequence of directory loads down to the target, since only one level's `Entry` rows exist in the table at a time. This is new logic; nothing in workspaces solves it today.

**The one real tree in the app** is the document viewer's JSON/XML tree (`internal/ui/viewer/tree.go`), backed by `viewer.Flatten(root *Node, collapsed map[int]bool) []FlatNode` (`internal/viewer/node.go:58`) and a `collapsed map[int]bool` keyed by node ID (`internal/ui/viewer/model.go:85`). It supports single-node `toggleNode(expand bool)` (`tree.go:118-137`) driven by `←`/`→` on the *currently selected* row — but there is **no "given an ID/path, expand every ancestor and set the cursor to it" function**. Nothing walks up from a target node clearing `collapsed[ancestorID]` for each ancestor.

**The closest analog to a "jump to a location by typed query" UX** is the viewer's **`g` "go to line"** prompt (lowercase, not uppercase — `internal/ui/viewer/goto.go`):
- `activateGoto()` (`goto.go:38-43`) opens a prompt in the filter-bar's slot.
- `submitGoto()` (`goto.go:76-101`) parses a line number, looks it up in `rowOfLine map[int]int` (populated by `text.go:33,55` from the rendered pane's line→row mapping), and calls `m.textViewport.SetYOffset(row)` — i.e., it scrolls to a **precomputed row offset**, not a tree node; it does not expand any tree state, and if the target row is filtered out it reports "Line %d is hidden by the filter" rather than trying to reveal it (`goto.go:94-97`). This confirms the codebase's existing precedent for "jump to X" is scroll-to-known-offset, not expand-ancestors-and-select — the latter would be new.
- Design-history note directly on point (`.claude/rules/tui-layout.md:30-38`, `keymap.go` comment at line ~176): lowercase `g` in the viewer was explicitly re-legitimized specifically *because* "the jump takes an **argument**", which is exactly the shape a `G`-triggered fuzzy find in workspaces would also have — but that argument-taking exception was granted to a **lowercase** letter (`g`), not the uppercase `G` action letter, and it lives in `retiredAliases`'s counter-example discussion, not in the `actions` table.

**Other views checked, none relevant:**
- `oci_resources/registry_browser.go` — a checkbox/expand-groups picker over registries (`buildEntries`, `toggleGroup`), not a searchable flattened path tree.
- `internal/ui/forge/explorer/selection.go` — `cloneSelection.includes(path)` walks **up** a path's ancestors to test set membership (nearest marked ancestor wins, `selection.go:31-47`) for a checkbox-style multi-select UI, not for revealing/expanding a tree UI to a specific node. Reusable *idea* (walking `parentPath` iteratively) but not a UI-reveal mechanism.
- `internal/ui/security/inventory.go` and friends — flat findings/inventory tables, no tree structure at all.

**Conclusion for §5**: there is no existing "expand ancestors and select a row in a flattened tree" pattern anywhere in the codebase to reuse or mirror. The nearest building blocks are (a) `viewer.Flatten` + `collapsed map[int]bool` as the general shape for a flattened, collapsible tree, and (b) the `g`/goto-line prompt as the UX precedent for "a letter that opens a prompt taking an argument, distinct from navigation." Both would need new code for a workspaces path-reveal feature; workspaces' current one-level-at-a-time directory model is likely the biggest structural gap to address in the design.

## 6. Enforcement tests recap (already detailed above, consolidated)

File `internal/ui/keymap/keymap_test.go`:
- `TestEveryActionIsOneUppercaseLetter` (line 64)
- `TestFreeLettersAreActuallyFree` (line 79) — update if `free` list changes
- `TestNoLocalToggleShadowsAnAction` (line 94)
- `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` (line 108) — **must pass**; `G` already satisfies `IsAction`, so it would pass even though reused for a different purpose
- `TestNoBareLetterIsNavigation` (line 139)
- `TestOnlyThreeCtrlCombinationsSurvive` (line 169)
- `TestEveryLowercaseBindingIsDeclared` (line 197) — relevant only if a lowercase letter is used instead/also
- `TestTheCommandModeKeyIsReachable` (line 235)

File `internal/ui/keymap/announced_test.go`:
- `TestNoAnnouncementSpellsAnActionOutInFull` (line 54) — any shortcut announcement must write `keymap.Get` (or whatever constant), never bare `"G"`
- `TestEveryAnnouncedActionIsBoundInItsPackage` (line 72) — an announced `keymap.X` must have a matching `case keymap.X:` in the same package directory
- `TestEveryAnnouncedToggleIsBoundInItsPackage` (line 100) — for lowercase toggles

Both files walk `internal/app` and `internal/ui` (excluding `_test.go` and themselves) via `go/ast`/`go/parser`, so any new switch clause or shortcut struct literal added to `internal/ui/workspaces/*.go` is automatically picked up — no manual registration of scanned files needed, but the **meaning/semantics** collision between "G = Pull" (oci_resources) and any new "G = fuzzy find" (workspaces) is something only a human/design decision catches, not these tests, since they check vocabulary membership, not per-view semantic consistency.</result>

content.text:
Both research agents are done. Two findings materially affect the design and need your input before I write the plan:

1. **`G` is already taken.** Uppercase letters have one global meaning across the whole app (Rule 111) — `G` is `Get`/"Pull the image or tag", used today in the OCI/registry browser. Binding it to "fuzzy find" in `ws` would pass the mechanical lint test (it only checks the letter is *some* declared action) but would violate the actual design rule and create a real semantic collision. The only genuinely free uppercase letters are `J`, `Q`, `Z`. Alternatively, the viewer already has a precedent for a **lowercase** letter opening an argument-taking prompt (`g` = go-to-line) — a fuzzy-find trigger is the same shape (a letter that opens a prompt, not a toggle), so lowercase `g` as a *local* action-like exception in `ws` is arguably a closer fit than burning a global uppercase slot, but it's a deliberate deviation either way.

2. **There's no tree.** `ws` is a single-level drill-down browser (`currentPath`/`navigationStack`/`cursorStack`), not an in-memory tree — nothing today walks the whole workspace directory recursively, and nothing "expands ancestors and selects a node." Both the recursive path-collection and the "jump to a nested path" navigation are new code, not something to wire into an existing mechanism.

questions.question: Which key should trigger fuzzy-find, given uppercase G already means "Pull" elsewhere in the app?

options.label: Lowercase g (Recommended)
options.description: Mirrors the viewer's existing 'g = go to line' precedent: a letter that opens an argument-taking prompt, not a toggle. Declared as a local exception for ws, like the viewer's g and the two existing DeclaredExceptions().

options.label: Uppercase J
options.description: One of the three genuinely free global uppercase letters (J, Q, Z). Keeps it in the global action vocabulary as a brand-new action meaning ('fuzzy find'), reusable by other views later if desired.

options.label: Uppercase Z
options.description: Same reasoning as J — free global letter, new action meaning.

questions.question: What should the fuzzy search cover: the whole workspaces root, or just the directory currently being browsed?

options.label: Whole workspaces root (Recommended)
options.description: Recursively walk from the configured workspaces directory every time fuzzy-find opens, regardless of where you're currently drilled into. Matches the mental model of 'jump anywhere.'

options.label: Current subtree only
options.description: Recursively walk only under currentPath. Faster on very large workspace dirs, but you'd need to navigate back up first to search outside your current branch.

questions.question: Should the recursive walk include files, or only directories (repos/projects)?

options.label: Directories only (Recommended)
options.description: ws is fundamentally a project/repo browser — matching directory paths (including nested repo/project folders) keeps results relevant and the walk cheap. Mirrors the existing walkSubRepos-style directory-only traversal.

options.label: Files and directories
options.description: Matches every filesystem entry recursively. More thorough but much slower on large repos (e.g. node_modules) and results include many irrelevant file hits unless filtered.

306	// navigateIn enters the selected directory.
307	//
308	// It does nothing while the table still holds the previous directory's rows.
309	// A load is a Cmd, so holding `→` used to drill twice from one listing: the
310	// second press read the same row, pushed the *new* currentPath onto the stack,
311	// and the breadcrumb grew a duplicate — `devsecops devsecops devex devex`. With
312	// the cursor moved in between it was worse than duplication: a sibling of the
313	// directory just entered was pushed as if it were nested inside it.
314	//
315	// Refusing is the honest answer rather than a hazard to remember: the rows in
316	// hand are not this directory's, so there is nothing here to enter yet. `←` is
317	// deliberately not guarded — it reads the stack, not the table, and a listing
318	// it overtakes is dropped on arrival.
319	func (m Model) navigateIn() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
320		if m.listingPath != m.currentPath {
321			return m, nil
322		}
323	
324		entry, ok := m.selectedEntry()
325		if !ok || !entry.IsDir {
326			return m, nil
327		}
328	
329		// Save cursor position before navigating down
330		m.cursorStack = append(m.cursorStack, m.table.Cursor())
331		// Push current path onto navigation stack
332		if m.currentPath != "" {
333			m.navigationStack = append(m.navigationStack, m.currentPath)
334		}
335		m.currentPath = entry.Path
336		m.activeTabIndex = m.tabCount() - 1
337		m.pendingCursor = -1
338		return m, m.loadEntries()
339	}

341	// navigateUp goes to the parent directory
342	func (m Model) navigateUp() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
343		if m.currentPath == "" {
344			return m, nil
345		}
346	
347		if len(m.navigationStack) > 0 {
348			// Pop from stack
349			m.currentPath = m.navigationStack[len(m.navigationStack)-1]
350			m.navigationStack = m.navigationStack[:len(m.navigationStack)-1]
351		} else {
352			// Go back to root
353			m.currentPath = ""
354		}
355	
356		// Restore cursor position at the parent level after entries load
357		if len(m.cursorStack) > 0 {
358			m.pendingCursor = m.cursorStack[len(m.cursorStack)-1]
359			m.cursorStack = m.cursorStack[:len(m.cursorStack)-1]
360		} else {
361			m.pendingCursor = -1
362		}
363	
364		m.activeTabIndex = m.tabCount() - 1
365		return m, m.loadEntries()
366	}

12	// isHidden decides what the workspaces view leaves out.
13	//
14	// One rule, consulted by the listing and by the nested-repo walk both: what the
15	// view shows is what S and F act on, and two rules for that question would let
16	// a repository be a visible row and an invisible target at once.
17	//
18	// The consequence of showHidden is worth stating rather than discovering: the
19	// walk will then descend into .venv, .terraform and .cache, so S on a directory
20	// reaches whatever they vendor. What bounds the walk is not a depth limit — see
21	// walkSubRepos — but the fact that it stops at every repository it finds.
22	func isHidden(name string, showHidden bool) bool {
23		return !showHidden && strings.HasPrefix(name, ".")
24	}
25	
26	// enrichEntry populates git and project type metadata for a directory entry
27	func enrichEntry(entry *Entry, showHidden bool) {
28		detectGitStatus(entry)
29		if entry.IsGitRepo {
30			return
31		}
32		// For non-git directories, find every nested git repo, however deep.
33		found := detectSubRepos(entry.Path, showHidden)
34		entry.SubRepoPaths = found.Repos
35		entry.SubRepoSkipped = found.Skipped
36	}
37	
38	// detectGitStatus populates git-related fields on the entry.
39	//
40	// The reading itself is git.ReadStatus: this file used to run the four commands
41	// with its own execGit while internal/git counted the divergence again for the
42	// sync, and the MCP server (§3.38) needed the same answers a third time. What
43	// stays here is the part that is a *display* decision — turning `origin` into
44	// something a user reads and something a browser opens — because that is what
45	// the view owns and the domain package deliberately does not.
46	//
47	// GitUnpulled is as fresh as the last fetch, and nothing here fetches (D35).
48	func detectGitStatus(entry *Entry) {
49		if !isRepo(entry.Path) {
50			return
51		}
52		entry.IsGitRepo = true
53	
54		status, err := git.ReadStatus(entry.Path)
55		if err != nil {
56			return
57		}
58	
59		entry.GitBranch = status.Branch
60		entry.GitModified = status.Modified
61		entry.GitUntracked = status.Untracked
62		entry.GitUnpushed = status.Ahead
63		entry.GitUnpulled = status.Behind
64	
65		if status.Remote != "" {
66			entry.GitRemote = extractRemotePath(status.Remote)
67			entry.GitRemoteURL = normalizeRemoteURL(status.Remote)
68		}
69	}
70	
71	// extractRemotePath strips the server from a git remote URL and returns only the path.
72	// Examples:
73	//
74	//	"https://gitlab.com/group/project.git" → "group/project"
75	//	"git@gitlab.com:group/project.git"     → "group/project"
76	func extractRemotePath(rawURL string) string {
77		// SCP-like syntax: git@host:path — colon must not be followed by "//"
78		if idx := strings.Index(rawURL, ":"); idx != -1 && !strings.Contains(rawURL[:idx], "/") {
79			after := rawURL[idx+1:]
80			if !strings.HasPrefix(after, "//") {
81				return strings.TrimSuffix(after, ".git")
82			}
83		}
84		// URL syntax: scheme://host/path
85		if idx := strings.Index(rawURL, "://"); idx != -1 {
86			rest := rawURL[idx+3:]
87			if slash := strings.Index(rest, "/"); slash != -1 {
88				return strings.TrimSuffix(rest[slash+1:], ".git")
89			}
90		}
91		return rawURL
92	}
93	
94	// normalizeRemoteURL delegates to internal/git, which owns the rule since
95	// §3.42 needed the same host comparison from a domain package.
96	func normalizeRemoteURL(rawURL string) string {
97		return git.NormalizeRemoteURL(rawURL)
98	}

100	// subRepoScan is what a walk found, and what it could not look at.
101	//
102	// Skipped is the second half, and it is the one that decides whether a gap is
103	// visible: a scan that silently leaves work out is the whole of D59, and the
104	// footer had no number for it. A directory refused by the filesystem is not an
105	// error the user can act on from here, but "12 repositories, 3 directories I
106	// could not read" is a different sentence from "12 repositories".
107	type subRepoScan struct {
108		Repos   []string
109		Skipped int
110	}
111	
112	// detectSubRepos returns the git repositories under basePath, at any depth,
113	// and how many directories the walk could not read.
114	//
115	// It used to stop at three levels, and that literal was D59: a repository at
116	// `monorepos/client/2026/api` was invisible to S, F and A while the directory
117	// holding it browsed normally, and nothing on screen said a limit had been
118	// applied. A scan that silently leaves work out is worse than a slow one, so
119	// there is no limit any more.
120	//
121	// What bounds the walk instead, and why it is enough:
122	//
123	//   - It stops at every repository it finds, so a repository's own node_modules
124	//     or vendor tree is never entered. That is the prune that matters, and it
125	//     was always the one doing the work.
126	//   - It refuses to enter a link pointing back up the path it came by, and to
127	//     enter the same tree through a second link. That is the cycle guard the
128	//     depth limit used to provide by accident, and it is what makes following
129	//     links safe at all.
130	//
131	// Measured before removing the limit, on this machine: over ~/projects the
132	// unbounded walk was as fast or faster than the bounded one (the repositories
133	// are shallow, so both stop at the same places), and over the Go module cache —
134	// tens of thousands of directories with no repository anywhere to prune it — it
135	// took 283 ms against 37 ms. That is the worst case, it runs in a Cmd rather
136	// than in Update, and it is the price of not losing repositories.
137	func detectSubRepos(basePath string, showHidden bool) subRepoScan {
138		var found subRepoScan
139		var crossed []os.FileInfo
140		walkSubRepos(basePath, showHidden, &crossed, &found)
141		return found
142	}
143	
144	// walkSubRepos is the recursive helper for detectSubRepos.
145	func walkSubRepos(dir string, showHidden bool, crossed *[]os.FileInfo, found *subRepoScan) {
146		entries, err := os.ReadDir(dir)
147		if err != nil {
148			// Swallowed until now: a directory refused in the middle of a tree
149			// contributed nothing and said nothing, which is the same silence the
150			// depth limit was (§1.3 D59).
151			log.Printf("ERROR [workspaces] read %s: %v", dir, err)
152			found.Skipped++
153			return
154		}
155	
156		// Read out of the listing rather than asked for with os.Stat, and the
157		// difference is not small. Recognising a bare repository needs three names
158		// where `.git` needed one, and a failed stat apiece is what that costs on
159		// Windows: measured over the Go module cache — the worst case, tens of
160		// thousands of directories with no repository anywhere to prune the walk —
161		// the stat version took 334 ms against the old walk's 75 ms. The listing is
162		// already being fetched, so the same question costs nothing here, and the
163		// walk now runs it in 65 ms while finding strictly more. The price is one
164		// ReadDir on a repository's own root, and repositories are where it stops.
165		if holdsRepo(entries) {
166			found.Repos = append(found.Repos, dir)
167			return // don't recurse into nested repos
168		}
169		for _, e := range entries {
170			if isHidden(e.Name(), showHidden) {
171				continue
172			}
173			child := filepath.Join(dir, e.Name())
174	
175			// A real directory cannot close a cycle on its own, so it is entered
176			// without asking. Only a link can, and only a link pays for the check.
177			if e.IsDir() {
178				walkSubRepos(child, showHidden, crossed, found)
179				continue
180			}
181			if !leadsToDir(e, child) {
182				continue
183			}
184			follow, err := mayFollow(child, crossed)
185			if err != nil {
186				log.Printf("ERROR [workspaces] resolve %s: %v", child, err)
187				found.Skipped++
188				continue
189			}
190			if !follow {
191				continue
192			}
193			walkSubRepos(child, showHidden, crossed, found)
194		}
195	}
196	
197	// mayFollow decides whether a link may be entered, and records it when it may.
198	//
199	// Identity is os.SameFile rather than a resolved path, and that is not a
200	// preference: filepath.EvalSymlinks does **not** resolve a Windows junction —
201	// it hands back the link's own path — so a resolved-path guard sees two
202	// different names for one directory and never fires. Measured here on a
203	// junction: Readlink answers, EvalSymlinks does not, SameFile does. And a
204	// junction is exactly what the defect was reported against.
205	//
206	// Two questions, and they are different:
207	//
208	//   - **Pointing back up the path we came by.** Entering it walks the same tree
209	//     again, and again. Every directory the walk crossed is a prefix of the
210	//     link's own path, so the chain costs nothing to reconstruct — and the
211	//     climb goes to the filesystem root rather than to the base, because a link
212	//     above the base drags the base back in with it.
213	//   - **Already entered through another link.** That is not a loop but a
214	//     duplicate: the same repositories under a second name, and a second scan
215	//     of each.
216	//
217	// Only a link pays for any of this. A tree with none in it makes no extra call.
218	func mayFollow(link string, crossed *[]os.FileInfo) (bool, error) {
219		target, err := os.Stat(link)
220		if err != nil {
221			return false, err
222		}
223	
224		for dir := filepath.Dir(link); ; {
225			if info, err := os.Stat(dir); err == nil && os.SameFile(info, target) {
226				return false, nil
227			}
228			parent := filepath.Dir(dir)
229			if parent == dir {
230				break
231			}
232			dir = parent
233		}
234	
235		for _, seen := range *crossed {
236			if os.SameFile(seen, target) {
237				return false, nil
238			}
239		}
240		*crossed = append(*crossed, target)
241		return true, nil
242	}
243	
244	// leadsToDir reports whether a listing entry leads to a directory, following a
245	// symbolic link or a Windows junction to answer.
246	//
247	// DirEntry.IsDir() reports on the link itself, so it said false for a junction
248	// pointing at a directory full of repositories: everything behind it was
249	// invisible to S, F and A, and the row rendered as a file — neither browsable
250	// nor scannable, with nothing saying why (§1.3 D59, cause 2).
251	//
252	//	entry a         IsDir=true   type=d---------  statIsDir=true
253	//	entry linked    IsDir=false  type=?---------  statIsDir=true   ← ignored
254	//
255	// The test is "not a plain file" rather than "is a symlink" on purpose: Go has
256	// reported a Windows junction as ModeSymlink and as ModeIrregular depending on
257	// the version, and os.Stat answers the same either way. A regular file costs no
258	// syscall, which is what keeps this affordable on a tree with no links in it.
259	func leadsToDir(e os.DirEntry, path string) bool {
260		if e.IsDir() {
261			return true
262		}
263		if e.Type().IsRegular() {
264			return false
265		}
266		info, err := os.Stat(path)
267		return err == nil && info.IsDir()
268	}
269	
270	// isRepo reports whether dir is a git repository, from its own listing.
271	//
272	// One rule, one implementation: walkSubRepos asks holdsRepo directly because it
273	// has the listing in hand, and this is the entry point for a single directory —
274	// the row detectGitStatus is enriching. Its one ReadDir is nothing beside the
275	// four git subprocesses ReadStatus runs immediately after.
276	func isRepo(dir string) bool {
277		entries, err := os.ReadDir(dir)
278		if err != nil {
279			return false
280		}
281		return holdsRepo(entries)
282	}
283	
284	// holdsRepo is the rule: what a directory has to contain to be a repository.
285	//
286	// `.git` catches a working tree and a worktree alike — it is a directory in the
287	// first and a file in the second, and neither is asked about. What it misses is
288	// a *bare* repository, whose HEAD, objects and refs sit at the root: that one
289	// holds history, so it is a scan target like any other, and leaving it out was
290	// the same silent omission as the depth limit (§1.3 D59).
291	//
292	// All three are required for the bare case. A directory that merely has an
293	// `objects` in it is not a repository, and calling it one would send a scan
294	// somewhere there is nothing to read.
295	func holdsRepo(entries []os.DirEntry) bool {
296		var head, objects, refs bool
297		for _, e := range entries {
298			switch e.Name() {
299			case ".git":
300				return true
301			case "HEAD":
302				head = true
303			case "objects":
304				objects = true
305			case "refs":
306				refs = true
307			}
308		}
309		return head && objects && refs
310	}
